chunks: Al-Shaykh, may Allah the Exalted support him, informed me from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from his father, from Muhammad ibn al-Hasan, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from Fadalah, from Aban ibn 'Uthman, from 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi 'Abd Allah, who said:

I asked Abu 'Abd Allah عليه السلام about a man whom some of the urine of beasts touches: should he wash it or not? He said: “He should wash the urine of the horse, donkey, and mule. But as for the sheep and everything whose meat is eaten, there is no harm in its urine.”

His statement عليه السلام, “There is no harm in the urine of everything whose meat is eaten,” is general and is not restricted to garments as opposed to waters; it must remain upon its generality in every state. Then he said, may Allah the Exalted support him: if impurity falls into a vessel or mixes with it, it is obligatory to pour out the water that is in it and wash it. The reason in this is that when water is in a vessel and impurity comes upon it, it becomes impure by it, because it is less than kurr, and we have already clarified that whatever is less than that becomes impure by the impurity it meets. Then he mentioned the ruling of a dog lapping in a vessel, and the discussion of that has already passed in full. Then he said, may Allah the Exalted support him: whoever intends purification with something from what we have mentioned, let him not purify himself with it nor approach it, and let him perform tayammum for his salat. Then if he finds pure water, he purifies himself with it from the state of ritual impurity for which he had performed tayammum, and he resumes whatever salat is obligatory upon him; there is no repetition upon him of anything he prayed with his tayammum, according to what we have already stated. The explanation of that has already passed in the chapter of tayammum, and in it there is sufficiency, if Allah the Exalted wills. Al-Shaykh, may Allah the Exalted support him, said: there is no harm in the compelled person drinking from impure waters made so by the admixture of carrion, blood, and what resembles that, but it is not permissible to drink them when one has choice. Drinking from them in necessity is not like purifying oneself with them, because purification is an act of nearness to Allah the Exalted, and drawing near to Him is not by impurities. Also because the one performing wudu and the one performing ghusl from states of ritual impurity intends thereby purification from impurity, and purity does not occur by means of impure things. Also because the person in a state of ritual impurity finds, for the permissibility of salat, a substitute for water, whereas the one compelled by thirst finds no substitute other than water for sustaining his life-breath; if he found such a substitute, it would not be permissible for him to drink what was impure from the waters.

What indicates the permissibility of drinking these waters in a state of necessity is that Allah the Exalted has permitted every forbidden thing in necessity. Do you not see that He permitted eating carrion where He, the Exalted, said: “Forbidden to you are carrion, blood, the flesh of swine, and that over which other than Allah has been invoked; but whoever is compelled, neither desiring nor transgressing, then there is no sin upon him.”

So He clarified that there is no sin upon one who partakes of these prohibited things in necessity. Wudu is not like that, because when pure water is unavailable, its obligation transfers to tayammum with earth; therefore it is not permissible for him to use impure water while his duty in purification lies in using something else. Al-Shaykh, may Allah the Exalted support him, said: if a person had with him two vessels, and something that renders impure fell into one of them, and he did not know which one it was, it is forbidden for him to use either of them for purification. It is obligatory upon him to pour them both out and perform wudu with water other than them. If he finds no water other than what he poured out, he performs tayammum and prays, and he may not use what he poured out from the two of them. The ruling of more than two vessels in number, when he is certain that impurity is in one of them without specification, is the same as the ruling of the two vessels. There has already passed earlier what indicates this from rational consideration and report, and that also indicates it.

key_terms.أَبْوَالِ: urines; here, the urine of animals relevant to rulings of najasah and washing
key_terms.إِهْرَاقُ: pouring out; here, emptying contaminated or doubtful water from vessels
key_terms.الطَّهَارَةَ: ritual purity sought for acts such as salat
key_terms.الْكُرِّ: the threshold volume of water below which water becomes impure upon contact with najasah
key_terms.الْمُضْطَرُّ: the compelled or necessitated person, such as one forced by thirst
key_terms.الْوُضُوءُ: wudu (ablution), the ritual washing for salat
key_terms.لْيَتَيَمَّمْ: let him perform tayammum; dry ablution when pure water is unavailable
key_terms.نَجَاسَةٌ: ritual impurity that contaminates water or vessels

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on impure water for wudu, drinking in necessity, and urine of animals whose meat is eaten?
ai.summary: This passage discusses rulings of ritual purity concerning animal urine, impure water, vessels contaminated by najasah, and the use of tayammum when pure water is unavailable. It also distinguishes between the permissibility of drinking impure water in necessity and the impermissibility of using it for wudu or other acts of taharah, supporting this with a Qur'anic principle concerning necessity.
